com: Judge. Greek, “instruct.” (Challoner) — The example of rulers is very powerful. (Worthington)
Therein. Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis. (Claud.) — As a whole city is infected with the vices of princes, so it may be corrected by their good behaviour, (continentia.) (Cicero, Leg. 3.)
Rulers. All who wish to live under just kings, Proverbs xxix. 4.
It, as he did David, Job xxxiv. 30., and Daniel ii. 20. (Calmet)
The scribe. That is, the man that is wise and learned in the law. (Challoner) — It also denotes an officer, Judges v. 14. God must give light and success. (Calmet)

Injury, out of revenge. (Haydock) (Leviticus xix. 18.) — “Cæsar used to forget nothing but injuries.” (Cicero, Ligar.) — This at least is the character of a great man. (St. Augustine, ep. 138., and 54.)

Men. It invades the rights of the former, and disturbs the repose of mankind. — All. Greek is obscure, “and from both proceeds injustice;” (Calmet) or, “it shall act unjustly.” (Haydock) — Pride attacks both God and man. (Grotius)
Deceits. Hence kingdoms are changed. (Worthington) — The ambition and luxury of subjects (Cato) and the negligence of the rulers, bring on confusion. (St. Augustine, City of God v. 13.)
Man. The desire of plunder, or of glory, occasions revolutions. (Haydock) — Covetousness is the root of all evils, and causes people to abandon the faith, 1 Timothy vi. 10. (Worthington)
Bowels, and would have no compassion for others or for himself. Some Greek copies leave out as far as sale, but Grabe replaces the omission from the Complutensian.

Beginning, or summit; arche. (Calmet) — Thus Lucifer and Adam fell by pride. (St. Augustine, City of God xii. 6.) All sin, being a contempt of God, springs from pride, (Prosper. contemp. iii. 3.) and from an inordinate self-love. (Calmet)
Sin, because man abandons God’s law, and falls into all misery. (Worthington) — The proud easily yield to all sorts of iniquity. (Menochius)
Disgraced. Greek, “hath taken an exemplary vengeance, and hath,” &c. (Haydock) — Them, as he did the giants, Sodom, Nabuchodonosor, &c.
Stead. Luke i. 52. (Calmet) — “Thales being asked what was difficult to be seen; replied, a tyrant grown old.” (Laertius 1.)
Nations, the Chanaanites, who submitted to the yoke: or rather the Hebrews. (Calmet) — Greek, “instead of them.”
Foundation: overturning Sodom, Babylon, and even Jerusalem, for their sins. (Calmet)

Wise. When Diogenes was exposed to sale, and asked what he could do, he answered, “I know how to command free men.” (Laertius 6.) — Joseph and Daniel obtained authority by their wise conduct. (Calmet)
Desert. Let not avarice deprive thee of the necessities of life, nor do any thing beneath thy dignity, Luke xxi. 19.
Glorified. Greek, “honoured on account of his knowledge, and the rich is, ” &c. (Haydock)
And. Greek omits this sentence: (Calmet) yet Grabe has, And the man who is without honour in wealth, how much more so will he be in poverty? (Haydock) (Ecclesiastes vii. 12.)
Judge his people.... In the Greek it is, instruct his people.
The scribe.... That is, the man that is wise and learned in the law.
fa: … For he will feel like one of the common sort, not accounting all men's possessions to be his, but himself to be one of all; and when spoiling all men's goods, thinks himself to have less than any. For measuring the things present by his desire for those whereof he is not yet possessed, he will account the former nothing compared to the latter. Wherefore also one saith, "There is not a more wicked thing than a covetous man." …
Tractates on the Gospel of John

And hence what is said of proud mortal man, clad in the tattered rags of the flesh, weighed down with the weight of a corruptible body, and withal extolling himself, and forgetting with what skin-coat he is clothed,-what, I ask, saith the Scripture to him? "Why is dust and ashes proud? Why proud! Let the Scripture tell why. "Because in his life he put forth his inmost parts. What is "put forth," but "threw afar off"? This is to go forth away. For to enter within, is to long after the inmost parts; to put forth the inmost parts, is to go forth away. The proud man puts forth the inmost parts, the humble man earnestly desires the inmost parts. …

… Let the humble hear from the authoritative voice of the Truth, "Every one that humbleth himself shall be exalted. Let the haughty hear, "Every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled. Let the humble hear, "Humility goeth before glory;" let the haughty hear, "The spirit is exalted before a fall. Let the humble hear, "Unto whom shall I have respect, but to him that is humble and quiet, and that trembleth at my words? Let the haughty hear, "Why is earth and ashes proud? Let the humble hear, "God hath respect unto the things that are humble. Let the haughty hear, "And lofty things He knoweth afar off. …

By the merchants of the earth we can understand the lovers of this world, who hand over their souls to destruction for the gaining of money. Of merchants of this sort Jesus, son of Sirach, speaks, saying: For this man has made his soul for sale; for in his lifetime he cast forth his innermost being (Sirach 10:10). He has made his soul for sale, who did not fear to hand it over to demons for the gaining of money;
Tractates on the Gospel of John

I am afraid that the reason why the soul went forth away from God is, that it was proud; nay, I do not doubt it. For it is written, "Pride is the beginning of all sin; and the beginning of man's pride is a falling away from God." It is written, it is firm and sure, it is true.
